Implement a feature in the Kodely codebase at C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 App Router + Prisma + Postgres). Work on `main` in that directory.

FEATURE: Content moderation on publish.

Why it matters: Kodely HOSTS what it generates on *.kodely.site subdomains, so a phishing page or brand-clone becomes Kodely's liability (IP blocklisting, upstream depeering). Today the publish path runs ONLY `scanForSecrets` (see `lib/secret-scan.ts` and `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts`). There is no abuse check anywhere.

IMPORTANT CONTEXT — read `lib/rate-limit.ts` first. Its comments explicitly say the existing limits are volume gates, NOT content moderation, and that the team deliberately refused to fake moderation with a weak heuristic. Respect that judgement: do NOT ship a naive keyword blocklist that pretends to be a classifier and will mostly produce false positives on legitimate sites.

WHAT TO BUILD
`lib/moderation.ts` plus wiring into the publish route, structured as a HIGH-PRECISION signal layer, not a verdict machine:
1. Detect the specific, checkable abuse patterns the board names: brand impersonation (a login form whose branding/wordmark targets a known third-party brand), credential-harvesting forms (password inputs posting off-origin or to a suspicious handler), and crypto-drainer / wallet-connect patterns.
2. Return a structured result — a list of {rule, severity, evidence snippet} — NOT a boolean. Follow the shape and spirit of `lib/secret-scan.ts`.
3. Wire it into publish so HIGH-severity findings BLOCK the publish with a clear, actionable error (mirror how the secret scan blocks today), while lower-severity findings are recorded but do not block.
4. Write the module so a real classifier can replace the heuristics later without changing callers.

Be honest in code comments about what these checks can and cannot catch. Under-claiming is correct here.

CONSTRAINTS
- DO NOT modify: `prisma/schema.prisma`, `lib/credits.ts`, `lib/agent.ts`, `lib/agent-sdk.ts`, `lib/build-site.ts`, `deploy.sh`, `.env`. Other agents are in this repo concurrently.
- If you feel you need a DB column to record findings, DO NOT add one — describe what you'd want in your report instead.
- DO NOT run `npm run build`. DO run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint <changed files>` clean.
- DO NOT commit, push, or deploy. Leave changes in the working tree.

VERIFY: write throwaway checks (delete them afterwards) proving a realistic phishing-style page trips a HIGH rule AND that several legitimate generated sites — a coffee shop with a newsletter signup, a pilates studio with a booking form, a SaaS landing page with a login link — do NOT. False positives on legitimate sites are the main failure mode; state your false-positive reasoning explicitly.

Report: files added/changed, the rules you implemented, your false-positive testing, what you deliberately did not attempt, and any DB column you'd want. Your final message is a report for me, not the user.

All tests pass, with the FP-trap correctly downgraded to LOW since the distance between "Sign in to your account" and "Netflix" exceeded the 160-char window — though this feels fragile if layout shifted them closer. I want to harden this by adding benign context prefixes like "streaming on", "now on", "as seen on", generalizing the pattern rather than enumerating every verb.

Actually a broad preposition pattern risks false positives too, like "sign in to your Microsoft account" being legitimate. I'm reconsidering the approach: instead of just checking brand proximity to any solicitation phrase, I should require directionality — phishing pages typically embed the brand inside the solicitation phrase itself, like "Sign in to your Microsoft account" or "Confirm your Apple ID". So I'm tightening the window to 60 chars and requiring either "solicitation...brand" or "brand...solicitation" within that tighter radius, then checking this against my fixtures.

Testing against my PayPal fixture, the gap between the brand name and "Your account has been limited" is tight but workable at 60 chars, though this feels fragile against real JSX or minified noise between elements — 160 chars is safer for detection but raises false-positive risk. So instead I'm keeping the 160-char window but adding a cheaper structural guard: stripping JSX/JS noise first and computing proximity over a "text projection" of the file built from string literals and JSX text children, rather than raw source.

Building that full text projection is a bigger change with its own bugs and loses original indices for evidence, so a more pragmatic middle ground is to keep raw-content matching but strip className/style attribute values before matching, since Tailwind class strings are the biggest source of intervening noise — this should let me tighten the window to around 110 chars without losing real detections, while also shrinking the false-positive surface.

Since stripping shifts indices, I'll just run matching and pull evidence from the stripped text itself rather than maintaining an index mapping — it's still readable, arguably cleaner. I'm writing a regex to strip className/class/style attribute values (quoted or templated) while leaving JSX expression-style className={...} untouched since those could contain meaningful logic.

Testing this against my cases: Microsoft stays adjacent, PayPal's stripped markup shrinks to about 25 characters which fits the window, but the film blog's form still runs several hundred characters even after stripping, putting the Netflix mention well past the 120-character window I'm tuning to.

I'll add a separate radius constant for brand-window checks, keeping the wider one for seed/input proximity, and also whitelist a few more benign prefixes like "streaming on" and "as seen on" before implementing.

## Shape

`moderateForPublish(files)` → `{ provider, findings[] }` where each finding is `{ rule, severity, path, evidence, note }`. It returns signals, never a verdict; `blockingFindings()` filters to `high` and the *route* applies policy. The analyzer sits behind a `ModerationProvider` interface with `setModerationProvider()`, and `moderateForPublish` is `async` even though the heuristics are pure CPU — that's the seam so a model/vendor call drops in without any caller changing.

Publish now blocks on `high` with a message naming the file, the reason, and the evidence, mirroring the secret-scan block. Sub-`high` findings are `console.warn`-logged and publish proceeds.

## Rules

HIGH (blocking) — each requires a conjunction, never a single token:
- `brand-impersonation-credential-form` — file collects a password **AND** names a third-party brand **AND** solicits credentials in second person within 120 chars **AND** the brand isn't in an OAuth/integration/credit position.
- `credential-exfil-channel` — password field submitting to a Telegram bot, Discord webhook, off-origin `.php` collector (file-scope), or to formsubmit.co / `mailto:` **within the same form** (900 chars).
- `wallet-seed-phrase-capture` — seed/recovery-phrase/mnemonic/private-key wording with an `<input>`/`<textarea>` within 220 chars; downgraded to `low` if the surrounding copy reads as a "never share this" warning.
- `wallet-drainer-approval` — wallet connect **AND** an asset-*delegation* primitive (`setApprovalForAll`, `increaseAllowance`, unlimited allowance, Permit signature, `transferFrom`), by name or by raw 4-byte selector.

MEDIUM: `credential-post-off-origin`, `runtime-obfuscated-payload`. LOW: `password-form-on-static-site`, `brand-mention-near-credential-form`, `wallet-connect-present`.

Two deliberate non-rules worth flagging: `eth_sendTransaction` with a fixed value is **excluded** (that's a donate button, not a drainer), and bare "Sign in"/"Log in" is **excluded** from the solicitation pattern — it's a nav label, and it was the single largest FP source while tuning.

## Verification (throwaway, deleted)

13 fixtures, each run twice: as `.tsx` source, and as **real `vite build` output** from the actual foundation at `C:\Users\edmem\kodely-foundation`. That second pass mattered — see below.

Abuse (all tripped ≥1 HIGH in both forms): Microsoft 365 clone → Telegram drop; PayPal "account limited" → off-origin `.php`; airdrop drainer (wallet + seed box); NFT-mint `setApprovalForAll` sweep with no seed phrase; webmail clone → formsubmit.co.

Legitimate (zero HIGH in both forms): coffee shop w/ newsletter (formsubmit.co, Instagram/Facebook/Spotify footer, "apple crumble" and "steamed milk" on the menu); pilates studio booking form + member-login *link* + "We accept Apple Pay"; SaaS landing page w/ "Log in" nav + Dropbox/Google Drive integration copy; **a real product login page** (password + "Continue with Google" + "Continue with Apple" + POST to own API) — only MEDIUM/LOW; crypto-safety explainer ("never share your seed phrase" + ETH donate button); film blog w/ member login + "now streaming on Netflix" + Instagram/TikTok; estate-agency portal login ("Sign in to your account", "session has expired", password, no third-party brand); art gallery with a formsubmit.co contact form **and** a separate staff login.

**False-positive reasoning.** The discriminator is that Kodely ships static builds with no backend, so a password field is already anomalous — but mock login UIs and real product login pages are legitimate, so a password field alone is only `low`. Every HIGH therefore needs a *second, independent* leg. Three specific traps I built and closed:
1. *"Sign in with Google" next to a password form* — the canonical legit login page. Closed by tightening every brand pattern below the bare name (`google account`, not `google`) plus a benign-context prefix list (`with|via|powered by|integrates with|streaming on|alternative to|…`).
2. *Brand and login form in different page sections* — real in bundled dist, where the whole app is one file. Closed by stripping `className`/`class` values before proximity matching, so the window measures text distance rather than Tailwind volume; that widened the film-blog margin from marginal to several hundred characters and let me drop the window to 120.
3. *formsubmit.co* — a normal static-site contact backend. Closed by requiring it within 900 chars of a password field; the gallery fixture (contact form + separate staff login) passes clean while the webmail fixture (password inside the formsubmit form) blocks.

Residual known FP: an educational page with a seed-phrase input in a live demo would trip HIGH unless phrased as a warning.

**One finding from the build pass worth your attention:** in the drainer fixture the minifier stripped the `/* setApprovalForAll */` comment, leaving only calldata — the name-based rule went silent on dist while passing on source. I added the raw 4-byte selectors (`0xa22cb465`, `0x39509351`, `0x23b872dd`, `0x42842e0e`, `0xf242432a`, `0x2eb2c2d6`) which survive minification. Anything relying on identifier names in built output is unreliable; that's noted in the code.

## Deliberately not attempted

No logo/visual similarity detection, no OCR, no domain-reputation or URL-blocklist feed, no drainer-kit domain list (goes stale, and staleness reads as coverage), no LLM call in the publish path, no homoglyph/IDN analysis, no cross-project or per-user pattern correlation, no scanning of `.css`/`.map`. No keyword blocklist — nothing fires on prose alone. And no attempt at an evasion-resistant design: string-splitting or runtime-assembled markup defeats all of this, which the module header says plainly.

## DB column I'd want (not added)

A `ModerationFinding` table — `id, projectId, publishedAt, provider, rule, severity, path, evidence, action ("blocked" | "recorded"), reviewedAt, reviewedBy, outcome` — one row per finding per publish attempt. Today the sub-HIGH signals go only to `console.warn`, which is enough to reconstruct one site after it's reported but not enough to query proactively. With that table you could: pull every `low`/`medium` on a reported site instantly; measure the real FP rate by reviewing `blocked` rows (currently unknowable, which is the main obstacle to promoting any MEDIUM rule to blocking); and rank users by accumulated findings, which is a much better abuse signal than any single page. A cheaper interim version is a `Project.moderationFindings Json?` column holding the last result — loses history but needs no new model.
